Clintonia umbellulata is an Appalachian native forming a low rosette of broad, glossy leaves from which rises a stalk topped with an umbel of small white flowers speckled with purple-brown dots in late spring, followed by shiny black berries in late summer that are a minor wildlife food source. It is closely related to the blue-bead lily (Clintonia borealis) but tolerates warmer, more southerly conditions and neutral to acidic cove-forest soils, making it a good companion for trillium, foamflower, and native ferns in a shaded native plant garden. Avoid disturbing established colonies, as plants resent transplanting once mature and take several years to flower from seed or fresh division.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; yellow mandarin forms slow-spreading clumps and is best massed with other native ephemerals and ferns rather than used as a single specimen.

Prosartes lanuginosa (formerly classified as Disporum lanuginosum) is an eastern North American woodland native with downy, arching stems bearing alternate, pointed leaves and small, pale yellow, bell-shaped flowers dangling beneath the foliage in mid-spring, followed by orange-red berries in summer that ripen to a rich red. It is a quiet, textural companion for trillium, wild ginger, and Solomon's seal in a shaded native garden, valued more for its graceful arching form and berries than for showy bloom. Give it consistent moisture and a leaf-mold-rich soil similar to its native rich cove and slope forest habitat, and avoid soils that dry out or become waterlogged.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in cool, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; rosy twisted-stalk is native to cool, moist mountain and northern forests and performs best in a sheltered, cool microclimate rather than a hot southern exposure.

Streptopus lanceolatus produces a distinctive zigzagging stem with clasping, parallel-veined leaves and small, rose-pink to purplish, bell-shaped flowers dangling on thread-like, kinked stalks from the leaf axils in late spring, followed by translucent red berries in late summer. The twisted flower stalks (the source of both the genus name and common name) and zigzag stem give it a wiry, delicate texture that contrasts nicely with broader-leaved shade perennials like hosta and ginger. It needs consistently cool, moist conditions and struggles in hot, humid summers or dry shade, making it best suited to northern and higher-elevation gardens or shaded, moisture-retentive microclimates further south.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in early spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, neutral to slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Japanese chloranthus spreads gently by rhizome to form a tidy groundcover beneath deciduous trees and shrubs.

Chloranthus japonicus is a compact East Asian woodland perennial with whorls of glossy, coarsely toothed leaves topped in spring by unusual brush-like spikes of tiny, fragrant white flowers made up of showy stamens rather than true petals. It is a refined, easy-care groundcover for a shaded border or woodland garden, tolerating typical garden conditions better than many choice woodland specialties, and forms a neat, low mound that pairs well with hosta, hellebore, and ferns. It is generally untroubled by pests and deer, and clumps can be divided in early spring every few years to expand the planting.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; white lily-turf is larger and more strap-leaved than mondo grass and makes a bold, coarse-textured evergreen groundcover or edging in warm-climate shade gardens.

Ophiopogon jaburan is a clump-forming, grass-like evergreen perennial with broad, arching, dark green (or white-striped in the variegated form) leaves and spikes of small white to pale lilac flowers in summer, followed by blue-black berries. It spreads slowly by rhizome to form a dense, weed-suppressing clump and is widely used in Gulf South and coastal landscapes as a shade edging, mass planting, or container specimen where mondo grass reads too fine-textured. It tolerates heat, humidity, and periodic drought once established, and old, tattered foliage can be mowed or sheared back hard in late winter before new growth emerges.
